1. Outside view. Historically, the Economist/YouGov generic ballot tracker shows high stability from week to week, usually moving by only 1 to 2 points at a time. Through July and August, the Democratic margin hovered consistently between +4 and +7. A naive extrapolation of the series strictly prior to September would predict a margin of around +6. However, the last two releases saw a sudden jump to +11 and +12, completely breaking from the summer baseline.

2. Inside view. The sharp jump from +6 to +11/+12 perfectly coincides with the traditional post-Labor Day shift in polling methodology, where firms transition from reporting Registered Voters (RV) or all adults to Likely Voters (LV). The provided search results clearly show this: an early September text notes that the 6-point lead was among registered voters, whereas mid-September texts quote the Economist/YouGov generic ballot at "D +12 among likely voters" and "up 11 points [...] on Tuesday." Furthermore, the political environment (an unpopular Iran war, low approval for Trump) structurally favors Democrats right now. Given that pollsters generally stick to likely voter models once they introduce them for the fall, the headline number will likely remain the LV margin. Thus, we should expect a number in the +10 to +13 range rather than a reversion to +6. 

3. Pre-mortem. If this forecast turns out badly wrong, the most probable reason is that the tracker reverts to publishing the RV margin (which would pull the number back down to the +6 to +8 range). Alternatively, likely voter screens can inherently add more noise week-to-week than registered voter samples, which could cause a sudden bounce down to +9 or up to +14 without any real shift in underlying sentiment. To correct for the (small) possibility of a reversion to the RV number or a noisy LV sample, I will slightly lower the expected mean and widen the standard deviation.

4. Calibrate. The series usually moves by ~1 point per week, but adjusting for the recent regime shift and the added noise of an LV screen justifies a slightly wider standard deviation. A mean of 11.5 and an SD of 1.6 gives a 1-SD range of 9.9 to 13.1, accurately reflecting the recent values while allowing a little room for standard sampling error.
